Interpret what the source says. For example, explain how deflation may lower investment.

questions.issue: Some shifted supply left or swapped curves, and many added written explanation.
questions.fix: Draw it clearly with the right shift and original and new equilibrium, and skip the text.

questions.issue: Some stated numbers only, and some missed that a country was not top for both measures.
questions.fix: Read the data carefully, use it to show the direct link and explain the exception.

questions.issue: Some just quoted the source, and some confused deflation with inflation.
questions.fix: Interpret each effect, such as falling confidence cutting investment, and consider good and bad deflation.

questions.issue: Some wrote about future demand, and some said substitutes make demand inelastic.
questions.fix: Define elasticity, then use substitutes, luxury status and share of income on both sides.

questions.issue: Some described merit versus demerit goods, and a few called education or health public goods.
questions.fix: Show merit goods are more beneficial than people realise, and public goods are non rivalrous and non excludable.

questions.issue: Some said one firm means a lower price without saying why, and some wrongly said it means low pollution.
questions.fix: Explain gains such as economies of scale, then the drawbacks of monopoly power.

questions.issue: Some said emigration would raise unemployment.
questions.fix: Link income tax to work incentives and demand, and corporation tax to firms cutting jobs.

questions.issue: Some thought hiring retired people cuts unemployment.
questions.fix: Retired people are economically inactive. Focus on skills and experience.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Candidates followed the instructions better than before.
Most candidates calculated the poverty figure correctly and nearly all picked a primary product.
Most identified a leftward demand shift when incomes fall.
The strongest answers used the data on investment and growth precisely.
mistakes: A significant number used facts not in the data, such as the effects of the pandemic.
Some calculation answers were the wrong size and had not been checked for sense.
Many left out labels on axes, curves or equilibrium points.
Some stuck to one side of a discussion, which capped them at 4 marks.
Many mixed up commercial banks with central banks.
fix: Base Section A answers on the data in front of you.
Check that your answer is the right size for the question.
Label axes, curves and each equilibrium, for example E1 and E2.
Discuss both sides when the command word is discuss.
Keep commercial banks, which lend to firms and government, separate from central banks.

questions.issue: Many left axes, curves or equilibrium labels off.
questions.fix: Label every part, including both equilibria.

questions.issue: Weaker answers speculated about the economy instead of reading the graph.
questions.fix: Describe the direct link using years from the data.

questions.issue: Some covered only one side, so marks were capped at 4.
questions.fix: Cover benefits such as more skills, and drawbacks such as high fees and inequality.

questions.issue: Weaker answers wrote on inflation in general or on tourism only.
questions.fix: Cover imports and cost-push inflation, then exports and jobs.

questions.issue: Many confused commercial banks with central banks.
questions.fix: Focus on loans to firms and government that fund investment.

questions.issue: Many confused stages of production with sectors.
questions.fix: Define horizontal and vertical mergers by stage of production.

questions.issue: Many answered about demand.
questions.fix: Give supply factors such as lower costs, productivity or weather and show a rightward shift.

questions.issue: Many treated a market as the whole economy and wrote about factors or sectors. Price was rarely mentioned.
questions.fix: Explain buyers, sellers and the price signals that lead to equilibrium.

quote.text: There will always be a relationship

takeaways: On a data table or chart, name the relationship, give evidence and then explain why it exists. Listing examples without a reason loses marks.
Answer from the point of view the question gives. Some candidates wrote about the economy when the question was about consumers, or about disadvantages when asked for advantages.
Eight mark discussion questions need two sides with explanation. Statements with no reasons stay in Level 1.
When asked to draw a diagram, just draw it. Do not write an explanation, and label the key price or equilibrium points.
Be precise on short definitions. A few exact words earn the mark, such as percentage change or output.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Six questions were answered correctly by 70 per cent or more of candidates, from different parts of the syllabus.
mistakes: Most picked an item that is not capital in the economic sense.
Nearly half may have mixed up inelastic and elastic supply when judging how much price rises.
Only a fifth recognised that unchanged revenue after a price cut means unitary elasticity.
Many did not see that inflation affects all firms, so it cannot explain differences in earnings.
Many did not link subsistence farming to low capital investment.
fix: Capital means anything used as an input for further production, such as a factory.
The less elastic supply is, the more price rises when demand rises.
If revenue stays the same after a price change, elasticity of demand is unitary.
Use differences between firms, such as unions or subsidies, to explain earnings gaps.
Link low capital and a labour-intensive method to subsistence farming.

questions.issue: Most chose an answer that was not capital in the economic sense.
questions.fix: Pick the item used as an input to make other goods, such as a factory.

questions.issue: Only 15 per cent were right. Those who chose the most popular option may have mixed up elastic and inelastic.
questions.fix: Low elasticity of supply means the supply cannot rise quickly, so price rises most.

questions.issue: Answers were spread across all four options, and only a fifth were right.
questions.fix: Same revenue after a price cut means the change in quantity matches the change in price.

questions.topic: Reasons earnings differ in an industry
questions.issue: The question asked which is not a reason. Many picked a cause that does differ between firms.
questions.fix: Inflation hits every firm, so it cannot explain differences.

questions.issue: Many miscalculated.
questions.fix: Find total cost from average cost times output, add marginal cost, then divide by the new output.

questions.issue: The most popular wrong answer was about people holding more cash, not about firms investing less.
questions.fix: Higher interest rates make big investments less appealing.

questions.issue: Answers were evenly spread, which suggests guessing.
questions.fix: Cyclical unemployment falls when government spending raises production, as a bigger deficit does.

questions.issue: Candidates split between two options.
questions.fix: Link it to weather risk, labour-intensive methods and low capital.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Four questions were answered correctly by 75 per cent or more of candidates.
mistakes: Many did not link longer storage time to more elastic supply.
Many wrongly thought a fall in interest rates raises the cost of borrowing.
Candidates thought monopolies attract new firms or that governments want maximum monopoly profit.
Candidates chose measures that do not raise the supply of goods as a supply-side policy.
Many forgot that inflation helps borrowers.
About a quarter chose primary income when asked about secondary income.
fix: Longer storage makes supply more flexible, so more elastic.
Lower interest rates mean cheaper borrowing and lower returns on saving.
Pick the supply-side measure that increases the supply of goods.
Remember inflation cuts the real value of debts.
Secondary income is transfers, while primary income is earned from factors abroad.

questions.issue: Candidates did not connect longer storage with flexible supply.
questions.fix: If a product can be stored longer, supply can respond more, so supply is more elastic.

questions.issue: Many said borrowing gets dearer.
questions.fix: A fall in rates cuts the cost of borrowing and the return on saving.

questions.issue: Candidates picked options that clash with a government keeping inflation down.
questions.fix: Check whether a government would want that outcome. It would not want higher prices or maximum profits.

questions.issue: Many picked measures that do not increase the supply of goods.
questions.fix: Choose the measure that raises production capacity.

questions.issue: Nearly half chose the wrong group.
questions.fix: Borrowers repay in money that is worth less, so they gain.

questions.issue: Only 19 per cent were right, and about a quarter chose primary income.
questions.fix: Secondary income is transfers such as aid. Primary income is earned from factors abroad.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Overall performance on the compulsory question was good.
Most candidates gave accurate answers on the percentage calculation and named benefits of trade links.
Numerical data interpretation has improved, with strong answers using evidence and an exception.
Many used the source well on training and capital, and on how falling unemployment causes inflation.
mistakes: Some ignored the word percentage and gave a number in millions.
Some listed two advantages when asked to explain one, or wrote about specialisation in general.
Only the strongest answers said a progressive tax takes a higher proportion of income from the rich, not just a larger amount.
Some added a written explanation to a diagram that only needed drawing, and a disappointing number confused the curves.
Some reproduced data without interpreting it or wrote about the wrong variable.
fix: Read the command word and give a percentage when asked.
Link specialisation to the information given, for example greater skills.
Remember a higher proportion of income is the key feature of progressive tax.
Draw only what is asked and label both equilibria.
Compare the data across countries, name the relationship and explain it, including the exception.

questions.issue: Some gave two advantages and some wrote in general terms.
questions.fix: Explain one advantage using the information provided.

questions.issue: Strong answers saw the proportion taken from the rich. Others missed it.
questions.fix: Say it takes a higher share of income from the rich, and link benefits to the poor.

questions.issue: Some copied figures and a few wrote on population sizes.
questions.fix: Name the inverse link, compare countries, explain why and spot the exception.

questions.issue: Some mixed up the two and ran into trouble.
questions.fix: Cover effects on competitiveness and willingness to invest.

questions.issue: A number said it does not change without saying it is with output.
questions.fix: State that it does not change with output in the short run.

questions.issue: Unsupported statements, or only firms considered and not consumers.
questions.fix: Show how fewer firms affect prices, quality and economies of scale for consumers.

questions.issue: Some missed that it is the percentage change in supply, or defined demand instead.
questions.fix: Say the percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price.

questions.issue: Many confused lower capacity with lower actual output.
questions.fix: Shift the curve for lower capacity, and use a point inside the curve for lower output.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Many candidates showed sound knowledge, understanding and analysis.
Most candidates managed time well and answered in sequence.
Many answers in Section A took the source material and used it well.
Most correctly divided to get 12.5 per cent, and most gave a balance of benefits and drawbacks for consumers.
mistakes: A small minority wrote about the economy when the question was about consumers.
Some added disadvantages in an answer asking only for advantages.
Some gave several examples of a data relationship without explaining it.
Some picked industries when asked for capital goods.
Common errors were shifting a curve instead of drawing a minimum price above equilibrium, or leaving the price unlabelled.
fix: Keep to the point of view the question gives, such as consumers.
Write only about advantages or disadvantages, whichever the question asks for.
For any data relationship, give evidence and a reason, even for an exception.
Draw a labelled minimum price above equilibrium and show the surplus.
Explain what changed in the data and what caused it.

questions.issue: Common errors were shifting a curve, or showing a second price with no label.
questions.fix: Draw the minimum price above equilibrium, label it and show the surplus.

questions.issue: Some ranked countries without explaining.
questions.fix: Pick one relationship, give evidence, explain it and name an exception.

questions.issue: Weaker answers said lower prices lead to more demand and growth.
questions.fix: Cover uncertainty, lower profit, cut output and jobs, and the trade effects.

questions.issue: Most gave short term causes.
questions.fix: Link development to improvements in the factors of production.

questions.issue: Curves did not touch the axes, and some wrote lower output.
questions.fix: Shift the curve inward to show lower capacity and explain the lost resources.

questions.issue: Weaker answers were one sided or not about the city.
questions.fix: Cover both sides, including public transport and the effect on the city.

questions.issue: Fewer explained how it lowers both types of inflation.
questions.fix: Link it to dearer exports and cheaper imports and say how this cuts demand and cost pressure.

questions.issue: Fewer explained why people may still emigrate.
questions.fix: Give reasons for both sides, such as better growth abroad, family links and growth costs.

quote.text: A decision alone is not evaluation

takeaways: Define terms precisely. Vague phrases about keeping the business alive or running do not define a term and earn nothing.
Name the actual product or service in the scenario for application. Writing just product is not enough, and each point needs a different reference.
Analysis shows the effect of a point. Repeating the point, or adding a new one, gains no analysis marks.
Do not write mirror answers, such as primary is slow and secondary is quick. The same idea is credited once.
In part (e) and the (b) case questions, make a decision, give a reason, and say why the alternative is weaker.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Candidates found the paper accessible and most scored on the majority of questions.
Many suggested suitable business objectives.
Many gave correct characteristics of entrepreneurs.
Many saw how being ethical attracts customers, and many named controls over dismissal and discrimination.
mistakes: Definitions lacked precision, for example giving a feature of unincorporated businesses instead of the term.
Candidates repeated the same application or wrote product instead of naming it.
Many wrote about lack of finance when the question excluded it.
A significant number confused being ethical with following the law, and some gave liquidity ratios instead of profitability ratios.
Evaluation was weak and often just restated knowledge as a conclusion.
A noticeable number left some questions blank.
fix: Learn precise definitions and avoid replacing the definition with one feature.
Name the real product or service in each application point.
Read the instruction in the question. If finance is excluded, do not write about it.
Name specific characteristics, not vague ones like skilled or charismatic.
Explain why profit and cash matter. Profit can be reinvested for growth, while cash pays day to day costs.

questions.issue: Many gave just one feature such as unlimited liability. Weaker answers mixed it up with a sole trader.
questions.fix: Say it is a business with no separate legal identity from its owners, then add a feature.

questions.issue: Many discussed lack of finance, which was excluded, and reused the same application words.
questions.fix: Pick two other reasons, such as lack of experience, and use different context for each.

questions.issue: Weaker answers described the information in the chart instead of answering the question.
questions.fix: Give limitations, such as assuming all output is sold or that costs form straight lines.

questions.issue: Very few developed the limitations. A significant number confused ethics with following laws.
questions.fix: Treat ethics as choices beyond the law and explain the cost or limit it creates.

questions.issue: The hardest question. The weakest answers said profit pays wages and materials.
questions.fix: Say profit can fund growth and cash pays day to day costs.

questions.issue: Weak answers said it meant delegating tasks.
questions.fix: Say a manager gives a subordinate the authority to carry out particular tasks.

questions.issue: Many gave descriptions without naming the functions, so they could not be credited.
questions.fix: Name two of the four functions and apply each to the business.

questions.issue: Weaker answers discussed producing new items instead of selling them, though the business was a retailer. Evaluation was weak.
questions.fix: Keep to a retailer that sells goods, develop each way and justify which is best.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: The paper was accessible and most candidates showed good subject knowledge.
Parts (a) and (b) were generally well attempted.
Many answers on packaging were excellent, and better answers on distribution channels were well developed.
Many knew the public sector is owned by the government, and most understood off-the-job training.
mistakes: Definitions often lacked the precision needed for full marks.
Some candidates did not know topics such as economies of scale and hygiene factors.
Many reused the same application, or the same analysis, for both points.
Some added analysis to part (c) questions or application to part (e) questions, which earns no credit.
Many left out a decision in part (e), or did not support it with a reason.
fix: Know which skill each part tests. Part (c) tests knowledge, or knowledge and application. Part (e) tests knowledge, analysis and evaluation.
Use a different reference from the scenario for each application mark.
Name different ways when asked for two. Air pollution and noise pollution are the same idea.
Learn precise definitions of technical terms, including gross domestic product with its time element.
In part (e), choose an option, give a reason and say why it is better than the alternative.

questions.issue: Some confused it with start-up capital or capital spending. Vague phrases about keeping the business going were not credited.
questions.fix: Say it is the money used to pay day to day expenses.

questions.issue: Answers were vague, such as easy or low cost. Some compared it with other sources.
questions.fix: Say it need not be repaid but may not reach the target. Do not compare it with other sources.

questions.issue: Weaker answers showed no relevant knowledge, and a common mistake was writing about methods of production. Some left out the context.
questions.fix: Give a real economy, such as buying in bulk, and link it to the materials the business uses.

questions.issue: Many described why quality matters, or confused it with quality assurance.
questions.fix: Keep quality control as checking the product, then develop and compare it with another method.

questions.issue: Most scored all or nothing. Many missed the time period or wrote about a single business.
questions.fix: Say it is the value of goods and services made in a country in a set period.

questions.issue: Many repeated the point instead of analysing, and few used the numbers from the table.
questions.fix: Give a reason, explain why it shrinks the sector, and quote figures from the table.

questions.issue: A common mistake was naming ways to be hygienic. Others listed motivators, and many left it blank.
questions.fix: Learn the theory and name two hygiene factors such as pay or working conditions.

questions.issue: A common mistake was writing about training in general. Others mirrored advantages as disadvantages of the other method.
questions.fix: Develop points on the method, then compare with on-the-job training for a reasoned decision.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates were generally well prepared and most had time to finish.
Most identified two advantages and two disadvantages of being a public limited company.
Many outlined two reasons why training matters, and many showed sound knowledge of market research methods.
Those who applied answers to the case boosted their marks.
mistakes: The weakest understanding was analysis of company accounts and the difference between quality control and quality assurance.
Candidates tended not to apply public limited company points to the case, and some scored only half the marks.
Some candidates mixed up the explanations for quality control and quality assurance.
Some wrote about production or sales instead of the product development process.
Weaker conclusions repeated earlier points instead of justifying a choice.
fix: Apply each answer to the size and type of business in the case.
Learn that quality control checks the end product, and quality assurance checks at every stage.
Use the numbers in the appendix, such as the change in profit margin, to support points.
Develop two points well rather than briefly listing several.
Make a recommendation that weighs the options and says why the others were rejected.

questions.topic: Public limited company pros and cons
questions.issue: Some showed good knowledge but did not apply it to the business, so they scored only half the marks.
questions.fix: Link each point to the plans and position of the business in the case.

questions.issue: Some mixed up the two. Simple statements stayed at Level 1.
questions.fix: Explain each method with its cost and benefit, then recommend one for the business.

questions.issue: Some wrote about production and sales, which happen after development.
questions.fix: Stay on the development process, covering limits such as research cost and a benefit such as new customers.

questions.issue: Knowledge was sound, but only the best conclusions avoided repeating earlier points.
questions.fix: Explain which method gives the most accurate data and why the others give less.

questions.issue: Not all showed how different groups use financial information. The question asked for the appendix data to support the answer.
questions.fix: Compare the years and say what each stakeholder would take from the figures.

questions.issue: Some knew about trade unions but did not focus on benefits in the case.
questions.fix: Link a benefit such as pay negotiation to the case facts.

questions.issue: Weaker recommendations only repeated earlier points.
questions.fix: Weigh the benefits against each other and say which matters most.

papers.title: Case study
well: Many candidates were well prepared and showed good knowledge across the syllabus.
Most gave two clear advantages of specialisation.
Many understood the difference between selling online and selling through a retailer.
Internal recruitment points were generally well made.
mistakes: More candidates than before did not understand factors in choosing a source of finance, or barriers to communication and how to overcome them.
The same was true of how break-even charts help, and the effects of depreciation, tariffs and quotas.
Many listed four sources of finance instead of four factors to consider.
Many gave mirror answers, such as primary research is slow and expensive and secondary is quick and cheap.
Many answers stayed as simple statements, such as lack of feedback, and conclusions repeated earlier points.
fix: Read the question closely, for example factors to consider, not sources of finance.
Explain why a barrier arises and why it makes communication less effective, then say which is easiest to overcome.
Use figures from the break-even chart, such as the margin of safety, to explain how it helps.
Check which country the business sells in and which it imports into before explaining trade changes.
Make clear which country you mean when writing about price changes.

questions.issue: Some swapped the methods or gave mirror points. Few reached Level 3 due to repeated conclusions.
questions.fix: Develop each method's advantage with its effect on the business and justify your pick.

questions.issue: Many named sources instead of factors to consider.
questions.fix: Name factors such as amount, cost, business type and purpose, and explain how each affects the choice.

questions.issue: Some used mirror points, forgot who pays for delivery, or misread the question.
questions.fix: Compare the channels, think about costs for both sides and justify one.

questions.issue: The hardest question. Problems with the medium were hardest. Most answers stayed as simple statements and many conclusions just repeated earlier information.
questions.fix: Explain why each barrier arises and how to overcome the easiest one.

questions.issue: Weaker answers just said it shows total cost or total revenue without saying why that helps.
questions.fix: Say how it shows the break-even output, margin of safety and profit or loss at each output.

questions.issue: A minority thought a quota is a tax, or that the tariff applied to raw materials. Weaker answers did not name the country.
questions.fix: Learn that a quota limits quantity and a tariff taxes imports. Then judge which change affects profit most.

quote.text: Trade discount does not enter the accounting system.

takeaways: Discussion answers must fit the scenario. Read what the business is actually offering or deciding, and do not write a general answer on the topic.
Give both sides in advice questions and end with a clear recommendation, because answers with only advantages or only disadvantages lost the recommendation mark.
Many marks went on accounts that included extra items or left out the opening balance. Keep each account to its own entries.
Use correct wording and no abbreviations such as BBD, COGS or C of P. Name the account, not the book of prime entry.
Practise the calculations. The report says candidates must be able to carry them out accurately in the exam.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates understood double entry bookkeeping well.
Questions on examples of bookkeeping, double entry and the consistency principle were relatively straightforward.
Most candidates answered correctly on the question about the expense to be charged for the year.
mistakes: Some did not recognise that a credit balance on a sales ledger account is a liability.
Candidates took cash discount as a percentage of the list price, not of the invoice price.
Some were unsure what an agreeing trial balance actually tells you.
Candidates mixed up how control accounts are prepared, including using sales ledger accounts as a source.
Some did not see that a debit to the purchases account reduces profit, and some applied the current ratio wrongly.
Some thought a partner's current account would be credited with interest on drawings.
fix: Remember that a credit balance on a customer's account would be a liability.
Calculate cash discount on the invoice price after trade discount.
Learn what it means when the trial balance totals agree.
Learn where each total in a control account comes from. Take receipts from the cash book, not from the sales ledger accounts.
Use the current ratio rules carefully and check the working with the figures given.

questions.issue: Candidates took the cash discount from the list price, which gave a wrong invoice price.
questions.fix: Work back from the amount paid to the invoice price, then find the trade discount.

questions.issue: Some thought the journal corrected a credit purchase, and others thought debiting the same account was the correction.
questions.fix: Check whose account was wrongly debited and credit that account.

questions.issue: A significant number did not see that the correction reduces trade payables as well as trade receivables.
questions.fix: Work out the wrong effect first, then reverse it in both accounts.

questions.issue: Many found the two timing differences hard. A common wrong choice showed the balance as the cash book would, not as the bank statement would.
questions.fix: Adjust the cash book balance for each timing difference and show it as the bank would.

questions.issue: A significant number wrongly treated the individual sales ledger accounts as a source for the control account.
questions.fix: Take amounts received from credit customers from the cash book.

questions.issue: Some did not see it was discount received tied to invoices received, and others confused cash with trade discount.
questions.fix: Keep full records of supplier invoices so you pay in time for the discount.

questions.issue: A significant proportion gave the closing receivables balance when the question asked for the increase.
questions.fix: Find the closing balance first, then subtract the opening balance to get the increase.

questions.issue: Candidates applied the ratio wrongly, thinking current liabilities should be one third of current assets.
questions.fix: For a two to one ratio, current liabilities are half of current assets.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Some candidates understood double entry bookkeeping and picked the correct option on many items.
Candidates found the accounting equation and evidence of payment by bank transfer relatively straightforward.
Many answered correctly on net purchases.
mistakes: Other candidates did not have enough knowledge of syllabus topics or could not apply it to some questions.
Candidates thought total credit sales are debited to the sales account.
Cash discount and trade discount calculations on the invoice amount were mixed up.
Some thought bank charges explain why the cash book and the bank statement show different balances.
Candidates mixed up the effects of recording sales returns as purchases returns on gross profit and cost of sales.
Candidates thought depreciation shows an asset at market value.
fix: Credit the sales account with the total from the sales journal.
Work back from the amount paid to the invoice amount using the cash discount percentage.
Remember that bank charges reduce the cash book when recorded, so they do not explain the difference.
Think carefully about which account and which side is affected when returns are mixed up.
Show non-current assets at net book value, which depreciation reduces.

questions.issue: A significant proportion chose an option that debits the sales account with the credit sales total.
questions.fix: Credit sales account with the sales journal total and debit the customers.

questions.issue: Many deducted the trade discount from the amount paid, instead of working back through the cash discount.
questions.fix: The amount paid is a percentage of the invoice, so divide to find the invoice amount.

questions.issue: Candidates added or subtracted the corrections in the wrong direction.
questions.fix: Write each correction with a plus or minus sign and check the direction of its effect on profit.

questions.topic: Sales returns recorded as purchases returns
questions.issue: Candidates thought gross profit was understated or cost of sales overstated.
questions.fix: Check how each wrong entry changes sales, purchases and gross profit before choosing.

questions.issue: A significant number thought depreciation shows assets at market value.
questions.fix: Depreciation spreads cost and shows non-current assets at net book value.

questions.issue: A significant proportion thought a profit would be a credit entry in the disposal account.
questions.fix: Debit the disposal account with a profit on disposal and credit the income statement.

questions.issue: Candidates found it challenging and some thought ordinary share capital is directly affected.
questions.fix: Dividend policy affects retained earnings directly.

questions.issue: A significant proportion thought return on capital employed would rise after taking a long term loan.
questions.fix: A long term loan adds to capital employed, so the return on capital employed falls.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Discussion answers worth up to five marks keep improving.
The suspense account in the correction question showed improvement, with fewer candidates including all errors.
The loan advice question was usually well answered and four or five marks were common.
The majority of candidates earned the final mark on the last short part.
mistakes: Candidates wrote a general answer about discounts to all customers when the scenario was about regular customers.
Trade discount was often not deducted before the invoice went into the journal.
Entries in customer accounts and control accounts were reversed, duplicated or missing items.
Manufacturing accounts had items in the wrong section, and labels were poor.
Incomplete records answers used payments to suppliers instead of purchases, or counted the purchase of a motor vehicle as purchases.
Ratio answers were missing correct descriptors, such as percentage signs or the ratio to one.
fix: Read the scenario carefully, and write about the people it names, such as regular customers.
Deduct trade discount before entering invoices in a journal, and label each total with an account name.
In a control account, post totals only, not every invoice and credit note.
Put direct wages in prime cost and supervisors in factory overheads, and show work in progress separately.
Rebuild the trading account to find purchases. Do not use cash paid to suppliers, and keep capital items such as a vehicle out.

questions.issue: Candidates did not deduct trade discount, and used descriptions and missing dates instead of account names.
questions.fix: Deduct trade discount first, date the entry and label the total with an account name.

questions.issue: Sales were labelled as purchases, figures were reversed, and the opening balance was omitted or put on the credit side.
questions.fix: Show the opening balance on the debit side, sales on the debit and returns and discount allowed on the credit.

questions.issue: Candidates posted every invoice and credit note, did not total the bank payments, and left out discount allowed and the irrecoverable debt.
questions.fix: Use totals from the journals and cash book, and include discount allowed and irrecoverable debts.

questions.issue: Direct wages were missing from prime cost, supervisors were put in the wrong place, and the vehicle driver was included.
questions.fix: Keep non factory costs out, and show the work in progress adjustment after prime cost and overheads.

questions.topic: Reconstruct trading account from incomplete records
questions.issue: Candidates used cash paid to suppliers instead of purchases, or used a motor vehicle purchase in the workings.
questions.fix: Use the mark-up to find gross profit, rebuild the trading account to find purchases and leave capital items out.

questions.issue: Answers covered all customers instead of regular ones, said paying on time instead of paying earlier, and ignored one type of discount.
questions.fix: Discuss both discounts for the customers named, and link cash discount to earlier payment.

questions.issue: Candidates gave one figure for returns instead of two, omitted an expense, or got the direction wrong.
questions.fix: List each error with a plus or minus and show workings so method marks can be earned.

questions.issue: Many focused on liquidity and the ratios in part (a), not on why gross and profit margins differ from a competitor.
questions.fix: Discuss selling price, advertising and expenses and how each changes the margins.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: In the opening journal, most candidates put assets on the debit side and liabilities on the credit side.
Many candidates earned high marks in the manufacturing account.
Candidates with thorough double entry knowledge earned high marks in the journal corrections.
Many candidates knew how shares differ from debentures and earned good marks.
mistakes: Candidates left out capital from the opening journal.
Candidates thought double entry removes fraud and errors completely.
Cash book errors included leaving out the opening bank balance and the discount received, and wrong entries for the contra item.
Candidates tried a bank reconciliation instead of calculating the correct bank balance.
Inventory account, provision account and rent account answers included extra items and wrong sides.
Principle questions got definitions instead of how the principle is applied.
fix: Include capital in an opening journal to balance the assets and liabilities.
Say double entry reduces the possibility of fraud. Do not say it removes fraud and errors completely.
Start the cash book with the opening balance and record contra and discount received correctly.
When asked for a correct bank balance, calculate it with adjustments rather than a reconciliation.
Keep each account to its own entries and put the opening balance on the correct side.

questions.issue: Average candidates earned half marks because of missing opening balance, wrong contra entries and a credit balance brought down.
questions.fix: Include the opening balance, handle the contra on both sides and leave out credit sales.

questions.issue: Many prepared a bank reconciliation statement when a calculation was needed.
questions.fix: Adjust the bank statement or cash book balance for the items the question names.

questions.issue: Some missed that the business already bought finished goods and some covered only one side.
questions.fix: Use what the business already does, give both sides and end with a recommendation.

questions.issue: Very few were wholly correct, and weaker answers included receivables, irrecoverable debts and rent.
questions.fix: Show opening inventory as a debit and transfer it out at year end, then show closing inventory debited.

questions.issue: Candidates defined prudence and matching when the question asked how each is applied.
questions.fix: Say inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, and only the current year's rent goes to the income statement.

questions.issue: Some invented their own difference, and included an error that did not affect the trial balance.
questions.fix: Start with the difference given and post only errors that affect the trial balance.

questions.issue: Candidates found the error that changed both gross profit and profit for the year most difficult.
questions.fix: Check for each error whether it affects gross profit, profit for the year, or both.

questions.issue: Candidates used words like profit and general reserve, put dividend in the wrong column and totalled columns incorrectly.
questions.fix: Use profit for the year and transfer to general reserve, and put each item in its own column.

quote.text: a conclusion is not a summary

takeaways: Read the command word first. Identify needs a few words, explain needs two or three sentences, analyse needs a chain, evaluate needs a judgement.
Build chains of reasoning with at least two links. Jumping from the first effect straight to profit loses marks.
Keep evaluation inside the answer, not only in a last line, and always tie the judgement to the business in the question.
Answer about the right party. Several questions lost marks because candidates wrote about employees instead of the business, or the reverse.
On Paper 4, pick the two or three strongest points and join them up. Do not walk through every piece of data.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Most candidates defined intrapreneur clearly, and many understood psychographic segmentation.
The benefits of budgets were explained confidently by most.
Many reached 4 or 5 marks by analysing one impact of trade unions on employees.
Most limitations of capital intensive operations were applied soundly.
mistakes: Some candidates explained advantages when the question asked for a disadvantage, so they scored nothing.
A significant minority could not define indirect costs. They gave an example such as rent but no definition.
Weaker answers gave two or three benefits of budgets instead of one explained benefit.
Some answers on trade unions described the effect on the business, not on employees.
Sustainability was sometimes confused with staying in the market or with lean production, and some essays had little or no evaluation.
fix: Underline who the question is about before you write: the business, the employee or the customer.
Learn the definition of indirect costs, not just an example of one.
When asked for one point, give one point and develop it with two linked steps.
In 12 mark essays, remember evaluation carries 6 marks. Finish with a clear judgement in the context of the business.
Use specific context examples, such as a real producer and a real sustainability issue it faces.

questions.issue: Some candidates misread the question and explained advantages. Weaker answers gave one piece of explanation only.
questions.fix: Check the word disadvantage. Give one point and two linked steps of explanation.

questions.issue: A few answers just repeated the term, saying segmentation based on psychographic features.
questions.fix: Define it using different words, such as grouping customers by lifestyle, attitudes and interests.

questions.issue: A significant minority could give an example like rent but could not say what makes a cost indirect.
questions.fix: Say indirect costs cannot be linked to one unit of output or one cost centre.

questions.issue: Weaker answers wrote about the impact on the business rather than on employees.
questions.fix: Pick one impact on employees, such as pay or contracts, and chain it through.

questions.issue: Partial understanding of sustainability, weak context and very little evaluation.
questions.fix: Link sustainability to protecting resources for the future, use context, and end with a judgement.

questions.topic: Role of HRM in an airline
questions.issue: Some candidates made no attempt at evaluation, or made simple comments without airline context.
questions.fix: Weigh the role against others and tie your judgement to the airline setting.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Both contexts were well understood and candidates used details such as the type of business and sector.
Most gave a valid method to measure business size, the most common being number of employees.
Survey or questionnaire was the usual answer for primary research and it was mostly done well.
Most had a good grasp of sole traders and democratic management benefits.
mistakes: Profit and market size were given as ways to measure the size of a business. Neither measures a single business's size.
Many tried different combinations of figures in the break-even question and produced long, unclear working.
Answers on the limitations of break-even ignored the context or used different context.
Some candidates jumped straight to the end of a chain, for example from motivation straight to profit.
Judgements were one weak sentence at the end, or just repeated the analysis.
fix: Answer identify questions in a few words and give only one answer, because only the first is marked.
Learn the break-even formula and show clear working. Box or underline the final answer.
For explain questions, give the term, how it affects the business, and use details from the named business.
Write every link in the chain of reasoning before you reach profit or sales.
Make a mini judgement after each analytical point and justify it. Link back to your arguments instead of repeating them.

questions.issue: Some wrote full paragraphs or gave several answers. Profit and market size were common wrong answers.
questions.fix: Write one short measure, such as employees or revenue, and stop.

questions.issue: Candidates tried many figure combinations and trial and error instead of using the formula.
questions.fix: Learn the break-even formula, apply it directly and show every step.

questions.issue: Most ignored the context or used a different piece of it, when the earlier calculation was there to use.
questions.fix: Give the limitation, explain how it hurts this business, then use details from the data.

questions.issue: A number confused skimming with penetration pricing or low prices. Many made a weak judgement or none.
questions.fix: Learn the difference between pricing strategies. Give a recommendation, justify it and say what it depends on.

questions.issue: Some repeated the term, saying it deals with qualities. Some examples picked from the data were really quantitative.
questions.fix: Say qualitative data is non numerical, and choose an example that is an opinion, not a measure.

questions.issue: Many could not use the given market share to work back to the total market size.
questions.fix: Practise using the market share formula in different directions, not only one way.

questions.issue: Judgements were a single closing line and assumed the analysis was proof enough.
questions.fix: Justify your judgement by saying which arguments were strongest. Do not summarise.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Most candidates answered every question and time was not a problem.
Many used the case material well for context and for evaluation.
Most identified that zero hours contracts could cut employment costs.
Most correctly calculated market share and market growth.
Many understood fiscal policy as spending and tax, and monetary policy as interest rates.
mistakes: Some wrote long definitions of contracts that earned at most one mark.
A few wrote a conclusion on an analyse question, which earned nothing.
Many had only partial understanding of liquidity and thought it was about profit.
Some suggested unrealistic ways to improve liquidity, such as becoming a public limited company.
Some assumed higher sales meant higher profit without thinking about costs.
Some analysed current conditions instead of the specific policy changes, or mixed up income tax with corporation tax.
fix: Read the questions before the case study, then highlight useful details as you read.
Allow about 1.5 minutes per mark, so a 12 mark answer needs about 18 minutes.
Use two or more links in each chain of analysis and use numbers from the case where you can.
Do not add a conclusion on analyse questions. Limit two point questions to two points.
Put evaluative comments through the whole answer and judge in the context of the business.

questions.issue: Some wrote long definitions and a few added conclusions. Some disadvantages were about staff, not the business.
questions.fix: Give a brief definition, then analyse one advantage and one disadvantage for the business.

questions.issue: Liquidity was confused with profit. Some methods were unrealistic and some answers covered too many methods.
questions.fix: Define liquidity as ability to pay short term debts. Analyse exactly two realistic methods with context.

questions.issue: Some missed the percentage sign, rounded wrongly or used the wrong year's data.
questions.fix: State the formula, pick the right year, round correctly and add the percentage sign.

questions.issue: A few worked out the growth in the business's sales instead of the growth of the market.
questions.fix: Check whether the question asks about the market or the business before you pick figures.

questions.issue: Many assumed higher sales meant higher profit. Weaker answers copied the text without applying it.
questions.fix: Link changes to the data, remember profit depends on costs, and judge each change in context.

questions.issue: Many knew the formula but could not pick the right figures from the network diagram.
questions.fix: Practise reading earliest and latest times from the diagram. Show each step.

questions.issue: Many lacked depth on the tool and asserted benefits without any chain of reasoning.
questions.fix: Link the tool to resource planning and cash flow. Add a limitation such as outside delays.

questions.issue: Some analysed the current economy instead of the actual changes proposed. Balance was often missing.
questions.fix: Analyse each proposed change in turn and balance with a reason it may not work.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Candidates coped well with the timeline and appendices.
Most could identify aspects of a marketing strategy.
The best answers grouped the strongest positive points into one argument, then did the same for the negatives.
mistakes: Many went through the timeline in date order, which gave developed analysis but rarely strategic analysis.
Some tried to analyse every piece of data and ran out of time, shown by a weaker second question.
A significant number did not reach a clear judgement.
Judgements were generic instead of being about the named business.
In the advise question, some wandered into other parts of the business and wrote much of the answer for no marks.
fix: Choose the two or three most important points on each side and join them into one strategic argument.
Do not use every piece of data. Prioritise the most relevant ones.
Give a clear judgement that follows from your analysis and name the business in it.
On advise questions, give advice the business could act on about its future.
If you argue something is not important, explain why it is not important. Do not just argue something else matters more.

questions.issue: Many analysed data in date order. Few combined strands, and many gave no clear judgement.
questions.fix: Combine the best points on each side into two strong arguments. Finish with a judgement in context.

questions.issue: Some drifted into other business areas and argued that something else mattered more. The past data alone does not hold the answer.
questions.fix: Stay on leadership, weigh how necessary it is for the business, and give future focused advice.

quote.text: A conclusion should add something new to previous argument

takeaways: Answer the exact question set. Some answers drifted into demand instead of supply, profit instead of cash flow, or the business instead of one stakeholder.
Use the tables and figures in the case. The report says numbers are some of the best chances for application and many answers did not use them fully.
Spell out every step of a chain of reasoning. Naming an outcome without saying how you got there only earns limited marks.
Evaluation needed work on several papers. Give a supported judgement that answers the question, not a one line statement or a repeat of earlier points.
The thing I would drill first is knowing the difference between evaluate, which looks at what has happened, and advise, which suggests what to do next.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Subject knowledge was generally good across the concepts tested, and so were analytical skills.
Most defined public sector, channel of distribution and the Just in Case method correctly.
Most explained one product life cycle stage and one element of a business plan clearly.
In Section B, most could analyse two reasons for failure from lack of finance, or two franchise disadvantages.
mistakes: Some mixed up public sector organisations with public limited companies, and a small number mixed up Just in Case with Just in Time.
Some spent so long defining a business plan that they ran short of time to explain the element.
Suggestions to improve capacity use such as hiring skilled staff or buying machinery do not work in the short term. Others talked about waste without linking to capacity.
Answers on status as a motivator drifted into long descriptions of theories or were applied to the business, not the employee.
Some Section B answers stayed generic and theoretical with little context, and there was often a reluctance to draw conclusions or make judgements.
fix: When a question asks about employees, keep every point on the employee.
Keep definitions short so you have time to explain the point being asked for.
In Section B, use the named business and its activities in every paragraph.
End essays with a developed, contextualised judgement that links to the statement in the question.
Cover more than one stakeholder or option when you need to weigh them against each other.

questions.issue: Some candidates confused public sector bodies with public limited companies.
questions.fix: Define it as organisations owned and run by local or national government.

questions.issue: A small number of answers described Just in Time instead.
questions.fix: Learn the two methods side by side. Just in Case holds extra inventory for unexpected events.

questions.issue: Some wrote about reducing waste, hiring skilled staff or buying machines. None of these raise utilisation in the short term.
questions.fix: Pick methods that raise output or cut unused capacity, such as marketing, rationalisation or subcontracting.

questions.issue: Too much theory description. The analysis was often about the business, not the employee.
questions.fix: Use a theory briefly, then explain how status makes an employee work harder.

questions.issue: Some answers stayed theoretical, with no use of the business's features and no judgement.
questions.fix: Use the nature of the business, weigh internal against external finance and decide.

questions.issue: Some wrote only about owners, so there was nothing to compare and no real judgement.
questions.fix: Compare several stakeholders and their different objectives before judging how important one is.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Many had secure knowledge of labour intensive operations, partnerships and inventory.
Calculations were generally done well, with clear working.
Strong answers used both words and numbers from the tables as context.
Many built clear chains of analysis over time on dynamic pricing, cash flow and mergers.
mistakes: Some confused labour intensive with capital intensive and wrote about machines.
Limited answers often left out the step of finding 10 per cent of followers and used the total number.
Some defined value added instead of giving a way to increase it, or named case facts without the concept.
Some wrote about demand factors when asked for supply factors, and profit methods when asked for cash flow.
Some confused laissez-faire with democratic management, and dynamic pricing with skimming or penetration.
Some answers on the merger covered several stakeholders or the business, not one stakeholder.
fix: Show every calculation step, including the percentage of followers before multiplying.
Name the business concept behind a case fact, for example a unique selling point.
Link context to the decision and say why it matters. Use the table figures.
Explain every stage of the impact, not just the final result.
For cash flow, choose methods that bring cash in sooner or delay cash going out.

questions.issue: Some described general services, which fits the tertiary sector, and gave examples without explaining why they fit.
questions.fix: Say the sector is about knowledge and information, then give an example that shows that.

questions.issue: Candidates skipped the step of finding the right percentage of followers, or made slips with large numbers.
questions.fix: Pick the right table data, work out the share first, then multiply, and show each step.

questions.issue: Some confused it with skimming or penetration. Others jumped straight to lower profit with no stages.
questions.fix: Define dynamic pricing as changing price with demand. Write each stage of the effect and use table numbers.

questions.issue: Some confused it with democratic style or analysed other styles. Judgements ignored the specific business.
questions.fix: Judge whether it is the most suitable style here, noting it may differ by department or pay method.

questions.issue: Limited answers often gave demand factors such as the number of customers. Some did not explain the effect.
questions.fix: Name a supply factor, such as availability of staff or inputs, and say how it changes ability to supply.

questions.issue: Limited answers often described ways to raise revenue or cut costs and mixed up profit with cash flow.
questions.fix: Pick two methods that speed up cash in or delay cash out and use the cash flow table.

questions.issue: Some covered several stakeholders or the business itself, and the judgement drifted.
questions.fix: Choose one stakeholder, chain the impact for them and judge that impact only.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Many had accurate knowledge of the concepts tested.
Most used the case context to develop application.
Candidates generally showed working and stated the formula for calculations.
Stronger answers on suppliers and on information technology built chains of reasoning that used the context.
mistakes: Many repeated information from the case instead of using it to explain an impact.
Some added evaluation to an analyse question.
Some did not use the syllabus formula or left out the unit, such as days.
Many could not explain financial efficiency accurately. Some thought it was only about profit, others only about liquidity.
Many repeated table data to say one option was better, with weak evaluation and a conclusion that only repeated earlier points.
Many defined delegation as just giving tasks and did not link it to intrapreneurship.
fix: Use data from the case to support your point and explain why it matters. Do not copy it.
Use the syllabus formula, write it down and give the unit with the answer.
On information technology style questions, give both an advantage and a disadvantage, and stay on the area asked about.
Define financial efficiency as using resources well to generate revenue.
Choose two or three key factors for an investment decision and weigh long term against short term.

questions.issue: Many repeated case facts without saying how they affect decisions. Some added evaluation that was not asked for.
questions.fix: Use the case fact to show the impact and what the business might decide. Stop at analysis.

questions.issue: Some gave only advantages or only disadvantages. Some wrote about IT in operations instead.
questions.fix: Cover one advantage and one disadvantage, both about marketing, and link each paragraph back to the question.

questions.issue: Some did not use the syllabus formula and a few left out the unit.
questions.fix: Write the syllabus formula, show working and add the unit, such as days.

questions.issue: Many could not explain it accurately, and some described it as profit or liquidity only. Balance often used other growth factors instead.
questions.fix: Say it is about efficient use of resources to earn revenue, then balance with a point about the same idea.

questions.issue: Some used the wrong formula, did not give a percentage, or were unclear on average profit.
questions.fix: Work out average annual profit step by step and give the answer as a percentage.

questions.issue: Many repeated the table and asserted a winner. They covered too many factors and the conclusion repeated earlier points.
questions.fix: Pick two or three key points, develop them, weigh them against objectives and give a supported recommendation.

questions.issue: Most analysed delegation alone and never linked it to intrapreneurship. Many defined delegation as only giving tasks.
questions.fix: Show how passing authority to skilled staff could produce new ideas, and balance with what success depends on.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Many showed good knowledge of strategic management and applied it to the case.
Most defined strategic management, SWOT and PEST, and many developed those definitions.
Many used numerical data well and built developed chains of reasoning.
Some counter argued their points with developed impacts on the business.
mistakes: Some knew very little about topics such as financial statements, and relied on ratios instead.
Many wrote about what the business should do when the question asked how effective its past strategy was.
Many answers on financial statements covered what actions to take, not how the statements are useful.
Some copied the case or just wrote one line of justification.
Some evaluated on an advise question, or gave suggestions on an evaluate question.
fix: Learn what financial statements are and what each one shows, not just ratios.
Read the command word. Evaluate looks at what already happened. Advise looks at what to do.
Focus on two or three aspects and develop each with a chain of reasoning.
Include a developed benefit and a developed counter argument.
Give a clear decision and a reason, and consider short term, long term and consequences.

questions.issue: Many said what the business should do instead of judging past effectiveness. Some defined SWOT and PEST by naming letters only.
questions.fix: Develop the definitions and judge whether past strategy worked, using case evidence.

questions.issue: Many relied on ratios and wrote about what the business should do. Analysis of usefulness was often one sided.
questions.fix: Explain what the statements are, give benefits and limits, and judge how useful they are for strategy.

quote.text: Balances must always be brought down

takeaways: The thing I would drill first is ledger account labels. Name the other account involved, use proper narratives and always bring the balance down.
Show your workings in the space given, so a wrong final figure can still earn method marks.
On multiple choice, read claims about systems and controls carefully. A system can reduce errors but never remove them completely.
For evaluation questions, give a clear decision and weigh both options. The report says these were often answered well.
Answer the question that was asked. Several candidates wrote about one side only when a comparison was needed, or included extra items that earned nothing.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 14, 15 and 21 were answered correctly by more than three quarters of candidates.
The mean score was 16 out of 30, and just over half of candidates scored 16 or more.
mistakes: Many candidates linked sales revenue to the moment cash is received.
Candidates accepted statements claiming a computerised system makes records completely free of error.
Candidates saw that absorption costing raises inventory value but did not follow it through to the effect on profit.
fix: Recognise sales revenue when it is earned. For a credit sale that is when the goods are delivered and the sale is recorded, not when cash arrives.
Treat words like ensure or eliminate with suspicion in statements about controls and systems.
When a costing method changes, work out the effect on closing inventory first, then on cost of sales and profit.

questions.issue: Nearly half of candidates picked an option tied to receiving payment, forgetting that revenue is recognised when earned.
questions.fix: Ask when the goods were delivered and the sale recorded. Ignore when the customer pays.

questions.issue: More candidates chose a wrong option than the key because they believed computers guarantee error free records.
questions.fix: Remember that automation helps reduce errors through calculations and checks, but cannot promise records are completely free of error.

questions.issue: Candidates knew inventory value would rise but did not link a higher closing inventory to lower cost of sales.
questions.fix: Higher closing inventory reduces cost of sales, so profit rises. In a first year of trading the inventory figure is closing inventory.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: The two evaluation questions were answered in detail and often well developed.
Candidates could say how a business benefits from control accounts, such as spotting errors and preventing fraud.
Many started well on the draft profit correction and showed clearly what was added or subtracted.
Candidates explained the business entity concept well and handled the layout of most statements.
mistakes: Ledger accounts had wrong narratives and labels, such as writing credit sales or receipts from customers instead of the name of the other account.
Candidates forgot to bring balances down on ledger accounts.
Candidates left out the extra drawings when calculating interest on drawings, and put partner loan items into the appropriation account.
The reconciliation of the sales ledger and the control account often included extra items that did not belong.
Equity ledger accounts were often reversed, with debit balances where credit balances belonged.
Candidates chose the matching concept when the question was about prudence.
fix: Label each ledger entry with the name of the account that holds the other half of the entry, for example sales or bank.
Always bring balances down and write full words, not abbreviations.
Include every extra drawing in the interest on drawings calculation, and keep loan interest out of the appropriation account.
In a reconciliation, include only the errors that affect the balance you are correcting.
Remember that share capital and reserve accounts normally carry credit balances.

questions.issue: Candidates did not time apportion interest on a loan taken part way through the year. Goods taken for own use should have increased profit.
questions.fix: Work out interest only for the months the loan existed. Add back goods taken by the owner.

questions.issue: Interest on drawings was often wrong because additional drawings were ignored. Some used partner initials or called a loss a profit.
questions.fix: Include all drawings in the calculation. Use full partner names and label a loss as a loss.

questions.topic: Partnership statement of financial position extract
questions.issue: The partner loan was called a bank loan, current liabilities were incomplete, and few remembered the capital increase.
questions.fix: Label the loan as a partner loan. List all current liabilities and reflect the capital introduced.

questions.issue: Candidates used descriptions like receipts from customers as labels instead of names of accounts.
questions.fix: Label each side with the other account involved, such as bank, sales or interest.

questions.issue: Balances were reversed, narratives were wrong, and the rights issue was understood but not recorded in the ledger.
questions.fix: Put credit balances on equity accounts and use bank as the narrative for cash entries.

questions.issue: Very few candidates could calculate closing inventory using the weighted average method.
questions.fix: Practise working out a new average cost after each receipt and using it to value the units issued and the units left.

questions.issue: Many did not understand contribution, so they could not calculate profit when materials were limited.
questions.fix: Work out contribution per kilo of the scarce material, make the product with the higher figure first, then take fixed costs from total contribution.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Question 3 was the best answered question on the paper.
Ratio work was strong, and the price earnings ratio was the one candidates got right most often.
Candidates produced cash flow statements in good presentation following IAS7.
Nearly all candidates calculated goodwill correctly and gave a decision with support.
mistakes: Candidates could say how to create a general reserve but not why a business would create one.
Few candidates gave three differences between goodwill and a tangible asset, and some described only one of the two items.
Candidates used the wrong year's dividend in dividend yield and left debentures out of gearing.
Cash flow statements had wrong depreciation, motor vehicle outflows and bonus issue share capital treated as cash.
Journal entries showed the consideration as one figure, with no split between ordinary shares and share premium.
fix: Explain the reason for a general reserve, not just the entry that creates it.
When asked for differences, write about both items side by side.
Use the correct year's dividend for dividend yield and include debentures in the gearing calculation.
Do not include a bonus issue as a cash movement in the cash flow statement.
In the journal, show the purchase consideration as two credits, ordinary shares and share premium.

questions.issue: Many could state how a general reserve is created, but far fewer gave an acceptable reason for creating it.
questions.fix: Write the reason the business sets profit aside, not only the double entry.

questions.issue: Depreciation entries were often wrong and the bonus issue was wrongly shown as a cash increase in share capital.
questions.fix: Check depreciation for each class of asset, and leave the bonus issue out because no cash moves.

questions.issue: Some candidates only described one item. Most gave one difference and hardly any gave three.
questions.fix: State differences by comparing goodwill with a tangible asset directly, aiming for three.

questions.topic: Journal to record buying a partnership
questions.issue: Candidates did not split the consideration between ordinary shares and share premium.
questions.fix: Credit the nominal value of the shares issued to ordinary shares and the rest of the consideration to share premium.

questions.issue: Candidates used last year's final dividend and left debentures out of the gearing denominator.
questions.fix: Use the current year's dividend and include debentures in capital employed for gearing.

questions.issue: Some only wrote about one business without comparing it to the other.
questions.fix: Write a comparison that mentions both businesses and what differs in their cycles.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Performance was good, with Question 1 slightly better answered than Question 2.
Many candidates found a more suitable way to apportion costs than a per unit basis.
Cost increase and selling price calculations had many fully correct answers.
Candidates could say how a budget can motivate staff and gave appropriate reasons and advice.
mistakes: Answers on setting prices with a fixed mark-up were generally weak.
Some candidates did not apportion quality inspection costs correctly, and some gave the selling price for one product when asked for each.
Trade receivables budget answers did not carry forward the end of February balance or left out the discount.
The statement of financial position had few correct entries for the bank and retained earnings.
Fewer candidates could say how a budget can demotivate staff.
fix: Think about the competition in the market when you comment on pricing with a fixed mark-up.
Work out the selling price for every product the question names.
Carry the closing balance of one month into the next month in a budget, and include discounts.
Rebuild bank and retained earnings carefully when preparing a budgeted statement of financial position.
Give both motivating and demotivating effects when asked about budgets.

questions.issue: Candidates found a better apportionment method but gave weak comments on fixed mark-up pricing.
questions.fix: Say what a fixed mark-up ignores, such as the competition in the market.

questions.issue: Some did not apportion quality inspection cost correctly and some gave the price of only one product.
questions.fix: Apportion each cost correctly and give a price for every product requested.

questions.issue: Some did not bring the end of February balance into March, and some omitted the discount completely.
questions.fix: Link each month's closing balance to the next month's opening balance and include the discount.

questions.issue: Few candidates had correct entries for the bank and retained earnings, although many handled trade receivables.
questions.fix: Take bank and retained earnings from your budget workings, then check the statement balances.

quote.text: Some options are only partially correct.

takeaways: Mark-up and margin got mixed up on several multiple choice questions. Know which one a question gives you and convert carefully.
On ledger accounts, label every entry with the name of the other account, not a description of the transaction.
In decision questions, use the facts in the scenario, give both sides and then state a clear decision.
Show supported workings whenever you adjust a figure in a financial statement, and use current accounting terms.
General reserves, the provision for unrealised profit and ledger account labels were weak spots, so I would revisit them first.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Candidates did well on a large group of questions, including 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 12 to 15.
Questions 17 to 21, 24, 26, 27, 28 and 30 were also answered well.
mistakes: Candidates picked options that were only partly correct because they did not read the details fully.
Mark-up and margin were confused when working out gross profit and selling price.
Candidates took a discount as a percentage of the amount received, not the gross amount.
Candidates were confused about what a bank overdraft is, so their suspense account entry was wrong.
Candidates used the bank statement balance in the financial statements instead of the cash book balance.
fix: Read every option to the end and check whether it is fully correct, not just partly.
Decide first whether the percentage applies to cost or to selling price, then calculate.
Work out discount on the gross amount.
Check whether an item is a debit or a credit before you adjust a suspense account.
Remember that a bank reconciliation can help find fraud but does not prevent it.

questions.issue: Candidates found the discount as a percentage of the amount received, not of the gross amount.
questions.fix: Work back to the gross amount first, then apply the percentage.

questions.issue: Candidates chose an option that only described straight-line depreciation and missed that no more depreciation is charged on a fully depreciated asset.
questions.fix: Read the asset details. Once fully depreciated, no further charge applies even if it is still used.

questions.issue: Candidates were confused about what a bank overdraft is, so they credited the suspense account with the wrong amount.
questions.fix: Check the nature of each balance, then work out the direction and amount of each correction.

questions.issue: Candidates used the bank statement balance instead of the cash book balance for the financial statements.
questions.fix: Use the cash book balance in the statements. The reconciliation only explains the difference.

questions.issue: Candidates subtracted a fall in inventory from purchases and used mark-up when margin was needed.
questions.fix: A fall in inventory is added to purchases to reach cost of sales. Then use margin, not mark-up, to find gross profit.

questions.issue: Candidates did not realise total variable costs are zero when activity is zero.
questions.fix: Read the diagram from the starting point and check where each cost line begins.

questions.issue: Candidates found break-even revenue but did not apply it as 60 per cent of the revenue needed for the stated margin of safety.
questions.fix: With a 40 per cent margin of safety, break-even revenue is 60 per cent of the revenue needed. Divide break-even revenue by 0.6 to find it.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: Candidates did well on written questions, especially about computerised accounting systems.
Statements of changes in equity were well answered with accurate figures and labels.
Marginal costing statements were clearly laid out and highlighted contribution and profit.
mistakes: Candidates added information that was not needed in the credit purchases workings, or subtracted discounts received when they should be added.
Candidates struggled with expenses that had prepayments or accruals at both the start and end of the year.
Drawings, rent payable shown as income and the full disposal proceeds were wrongly put in the statement of profit or loss.
Ledger labels were descriptions, not the names of the other accounts.
Candidates misunderstood general reserves, often thinking they are cash.
In the vehicle disposal calculation, some got the carrying value wrong and mishandled the proceeds, so a profit appeared where there was a loss.
fix: Pick out only the figures you need and add or subtract each one in the right direction.
Work through each expense step by step when there are several adjustments.
Include only the disposal profit or loss in the statement of profit or loss, and leave drawings out.
Use the name of the other account as the label in a ledger account.
Learn that a general reserve is for future uncertainties and dividend flexibility, and is not necessarily cash.

questions.issue: Candidates included opening and closing inventory and subtracted discounts received instead of adding them.
questions.fix: Use only the relevant information, and add discounts received.

questions.topic: Statement of profit or loss adjustments
questions.issue: Candidates mishandled prepayments and accruals at both ends of the year, and included drawings or full sale proceeds.
questions.fix: Show workings for each adjusted expense and include only profit or loss on disposal.

questions.issue: Some gave advantages and disadvantages but no clear decision, or only repeated points from the question.
questions.fix: Explain what each point means for the owner and finish with a clear decision.

questions.issue: Labels described the transaction and the bank entry was merged with the disposal amount.
questions.fix: Label with the other account names and keep the bank entry separate.

questions.topic: Equity changes with bonus and rights issues
questions.issue: Candidates used dates instead of describing the transaction, and took the full revaluation from the reserve even though that left a negative balance.
questions.fix: Describe each transaction in words. Do not let a reserve go below zero.

questions.issue: Many thought a general reserve represents cash.
questions.fix: State that it is kept for future contingencies and can give flexibility on dividends.

questions.issue: Candidates stopped after the new selling price and did not calculate the increase asked for, or started profit workings instead.
questions.fix: Add fixed costs to target profit to get the total contribution needed. Divide by the units, add the variable cost per unit to reach the new price, then take away the old price to show the increase.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Many candidates showed knowledge across a wide range of the syllabus.
Accounts were generally produced neatly and in the right format.
Most candidates made the manufacturing calculations in question 3 correctly, including work in progress.
mistakes: Many candidates did not understand the provision for unrealised profit.
Written answers did not use the scenario fully to support the decision.
Some candidates left goodwill out of the statement of financial position.
Some candidates got the bank loan wrong or missed the movement in retained earnings.
Some forgot to take the factory profit off the transfer price when finding production cost, or left the factory profit out of the statement.
Some candidates struggled to name a relevant ethic.
fix: Revise the provision for unrealised profit, including the opening balance, the closing balance and the effect on profit.
Use facts from the scenario in every written answer and make the decision depend on them.
Include goodwill in the statement of financial position.
